title: Reading a whole work: method

objectives.can: Plan the reading of a whole Latin work: set the assistance level, use the word panel and corpus occurrences sparingly, and keep a list of constructions to revisit.

explanation.summary: Reading a whole work is a different skill from working through a sentence. You need a routine that keeps you moving, a way of asking for help that does not turn reading into looking up, and a list of what stopped you so that you can come back to it. This lesson sets out the routine and tries it on two real works, Cassian's Institutes and Augustine's On the Spirit and the Letter.

sections.heading: Read the paragraph through first
body: Take one section at a time. Read it once from beginning to end without stopping to translate. On this pass you are looking for three things: the main verbs, who or what they are about, and where the sentence ends. Ignore what you do not know. Cassian's Institutes begins with a question: *unde conpetentius … quam ex ipso habitu monachorum sumemus exordium?* The main verb is *sumemus*, 'we shall take', and the question is where to begin. Everything before it is the occasion and the manner; you can see that on a first pass without knowing a single other word.
Then read the section a second time, more slowly, and fill in the clauses that hang on the main verbs. Only after that do you translate, and only if you need to.

sections.heading: Mark what stopped you, and name it
body: As you read, mark the places where you could not go on. Then say what kind of stop it was: a word you do not know, a form you could not place, a construction you could not recognise, or a reference you could not follow. Each kind has its own remedy, and naming the kind is half of finding it.

In Augustine, *sciri enim facit peccatum potius quam caueri* may stop you on the infinitives *sciri* and *caueri*. They are passive infinitives after *facit*: it makes sin known rather than avoided. That is a construction, not a vocabulary problem, and the remedy is a note, not a dictionary.

sections.heading: Ask for help in order, and sparingly
body: Use the least help that gets you on. First the context: authors often explain their own words. In *operimenta, inquiens, non uestimenta … id est quae corpus operiant tantum*, Cassian himself says what he means, 'coverings, not garments, that is, things which only cover the body'. Next the word panel, which shows the analysis and the meanings of a word. Next the places where the word occurs in other works of the library, which show how authors use it in other settings. Last, a translation, if one is matched to the section.

The assistance level in the reader is yours to choose. Begin at the lowest level that lets you reach the end of a section. Raise it for a hard passage and lower it again. The aim is to need the help less each week, and that depends on what you do with it afterwards, which is the next point.

sections.heading: Keep a list of constructions to revisit
body: A short list of constructions that stopped you is worth more than a long list of words. Write down the construction, the section where you met it, and one clause that shows it. Return to the list when a lesson names the same construction, and take the forms to GoReview, where you can review them. The same few constructions come back in every long work: relative clauses with the subjunctive, ablative absolutes, passive infinitives, gerundives, indirect statement, and the *ita … ut* result clause that Cassian uses in the first book.

sections.heading: Know what the tool cannot tell you
body: Every analysis of these works is automatic. Many words are marked as provisional because the program could not choose between readings, and some readings are wrong. In *De institutis ac regulis monasteriorum dicturi*, the program gives *dicturi* as a genitive singular. The sense and the verb *sumemus* point to a nominative plural, 'we who are about to speak'. And in *cum exteriorem ornatum … depinxerimus*, the ending *-erimus* could be a future perfect indicative or a perfect subjunctive; the sentence is about what we shall be able to do 'when we have set out' the outer dress. Treat the panel as a first guess and check it against the sense.

sections.heading: Planning a whole work
body: A work is read in sections, and the sections of these works differ greatly in length. Cassian's Institutes is a long work in twelve books, each divided into small sections. Augustine's On the Spirit and the Letter is much shorter, but its sections are long, unpunctuated in some editions, and dense. Choose a pace of a few sections at a time, set it before you begin, and keep it. Read a section through, mark and look up, add to your list, and move on. At the end of a book, go back to the list.

misunderstandings: Reading is not translating. A first reading that finds the main verbs and the shape of the sentence is a real reading, and it is the one you should always do first.
Looking up every word does not help you read. It slows the pace and hides the pattern. Look up a word only when the context and the form leave you stuck.
A word panel is not an authority. The analysis is automatic, and a provisional reading may be wrong. Test it against the sense of the sentence.
A longer list is not a better list. Keep only the constructions that stopped you, and strike one out when you recognise it without help.

deeper.heading: Why authors explain themselves
body: Early monastic and theological writers often gloss their own words, especially when they quote Scripture in a Latin version that differs from another one. Cassian's remark that a form is not found 'in some Latin copies' suggests that the Latin Bible he knew had variant wordings. The note is useful for the reader: the author's own explanation is often a better guide to a word than a dictionary.

quoted.title: Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum)
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: The first pass finds two future verbs, *sumemus* and *poterimus*. *sumemus* is the main verb of the opening question, 'where shall we take our beginning?'. *poterimus* belongs to the next sentence, 'we shall be able to set out the inner dress when …'. The last sentence uses *oportet* with an infinitive, 'it is necessary that the monk walk …'. Three sentences, three main verbs, and the shape of the passage is already clear.

examples.analysis: *sit* is a subjunctive of command, 'let the monk's clothing be', and the relative clauses with *contegat*, *repellat* and *enutriat* say what sort of clothing: the kind that covers the body, and not the kind that feeds vanity. The author then explains his own word: *operimenta* (coverings), *non uestimenta* (not garments). The context gives the meaning; no help is needed.

examples.analysis: *praesumitur* and *tenetur* are passive verbs in a clause that begins with *quidquid*, 'whatever is taken up by one or a few and is not held by the whole body'. That clause is the subject; the main verb is *est*, with the predicates *superfluum* and *elatum*. Several other words in the section are marked as provisional by the program, so check the sense as you go: the point is that a practice held by one or a few, and not by the whole community, is to be judged excessive.

quoted.title: On the Spirit and the Letter
quoted.reference: Augustine of Hippo, On the Spirit and the Letter 8
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: *occidit* and *desit* are the key verbs: the letter of the law kills if the life-giving spirit is lacking. *sciri enim facit peccatum potius quam caueri* adds the reason: the law makes sin known (*sciri*) rather than avoided (*caueri*). Mark the passive infinitives after *facit* as a construction to revisit. The words *quemadmodum supra diximus* send you back to an earlier section of the work.

examples.analysis: *dicimus* takes an accusative and infinitive, 'we say that the human will is helped': *uoluntatem* is the subject accusative and *adiuuari* the passive infinitive. The *ut* clause with *accipiat* that follows is a long result clause. A first pass finds the main verb, the report it introduces, and the result clause; a second pass can fill in the details.

options: *sumemus*, a future verb whose subject is 'we'.
practice.explain: *sumemus* is the only form with a person and number (first plural, future), so it is the finite verb. *dicturi* and *donante* are participles, and *exordium* is its object: 'where shall we take our beginning?'

practice.explain: Cassian explains his own word in the same sentence: *operimenta* are things which only cover the body, as against *uestimenta*, garments. Context comes first, the word panel and other occurrences next.

options: *facit* with passive infinitives (*sciri*, *caueri*): it makes sin known rather than avoided.
A relative clause of purpose with *quam*.
practice.explain: *sciri* and *caueri* are present passive infinitives, and they are the objects of *facit* together with *peccatum*: the law makes sin to be known rather than to be avoided. It is a construction to note, not a word to look up. *enim* is a particle, 'for', and the sentence has no ablative absolute.

practice.prompt: *quidquid enim inter famulos dei praesumitur ab uno uel paucis nec catholice per omne corpus fraternitatis tenetur, aut superfluum aut elatum est …* What is the shape of the sentence?

options: *tenetur* is the main verb, and *est* belongs to a relative clause.
*praesumitur* is the main verb, and *tenetur* is a command.
*quidquid … tenetur* is the subject clause, and *est* the main verb: whatever is taken up by few and not held by all is superfluous or proud.
The sentence has no main verb.
practice.explain: *praesumitur* and *tenetur* are verbs inside the *quidquid* clause. The clause as a whole is the subject, and *est* governs the predicates *superfluum* and *elatum*. Seeing this takes only a first pass.

The reader should delete the section from the list.
The analysis must be right, because it comes from a program.
The word is a verb and cannot have a case.

check.prompt: *itaque monachum ut militem Christi in procinctu semper belli positum accinctis lumbis iugiter oportet incedere.* How is this sentence built?

quoted.title: Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum)
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: *incedere* is a noun and the object of *oportet*.
*positum* is a finite verb in the perfect.
*oportet* takes *monachum* and the infinitive *incedere*: it is fitting that the monk walk; *positum* describes him, and *accinctis lumbis* gives the manner.
*monachum* is the subject of *oportet*, which is a first person verb.
check.explain: *oportet* is an impersonal verb that takes an accusative and an infinitive, 'it is necessary for the monk to walk'. *positum* is a participle agreeing with *monachum* (accusative), and the ablative phrase *accinctis lumbis* tells how: with loins girded.

check.prompt: *quorum interiorem cultum consequenter tunc poterimus exponere, cum exteriorem ornatum sub oculorum depinxerimus obtutibus.* The ending of *depinxerimus* could be a future perfect or a perfect subjunctive. How does the sentence help?

options: The *cum* clause is a wish, so the verb is a subjunctive of wish.
The main verb *poterimus* is future, and the *cum* clause names what will have been done by then: 'when we have set out the outer dress'.
The form must be a past tense because *cum* means 'since'.
check.explain: The sentence says that we shall be able to explain the inner dress at the time when we have described the outer. That sense fits a future perfect. Ambiguity of form is common, and the context settles it.

check.prompt: *Doctrina quippe illa qua mandatum accipimus continenter recteque uiuendi littera est occidens nisi adsit uiuificans spiritus.* What is the core of this sentence?

quoted.title: On the Spirit and the Letter
quoted.reference: Augustine of Hippo, On the Spirit and the Letter 6
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: *Doctrina … est littera occidens*: that teaching is a killing letter, unless the life-giving spirit is present; *qua mandatum accipimus* only says by what teaching.
*adsit* is the main verb, and the rest is a wish.
*accipimus* is the main verb, and *littera* is its object.
check.explain: *est* with *Doctrina* as subject and *littera … occidens* as predicate is the core. *qua mandatum accipimus* is a relative clause on *doctrina*, and *nisi adsit …* is a condition. *adsit* is a subjunctive inside the *nisi* clause, a condition, and not a wish.

check.prompt: *quoniam legis littera quae docet non esse peccandum, si spiritus uiuificans desit, occidit.* What is the subject of *occidit*?

quoted.title: On the Spirit and the Letter
quoted.reference: Augustine of Hippo, On the Spirit and the Letter 8
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: *peccandum*, the thing that must not be done.
*spiritus*, because it is the nearest nominative.
*littera*, 'the letter of the law', which kills if the spirit is lacking.
check.explain: *si spiritus uiuificans desit* is a condition placed inside the sentence, and it has its own subject. The subject of *occidit* is *littera*, the letter of the law, with *quae docet non esse peccandum* as a relative clause describing it. Bracket the condition and set it aside, and the core of the sentence is easy to see.

check.prompt: *sic magis accipiendum quemadmodum supra diximus.* What should the reader do with *supra diximus*?

options: Note that the author refers to something said earlier in the work, and go back to find it if the point is unclear.
Treat it as a quotation from the apostle.
Ignore it, because it is only a verb in the perfect.
Look it up as a place name.
check.explain: *supra diximus* is 'we said above'. It tells the reader that the point was made earlier. In a whole-work reading, such references are the thread; follow one back when the argument is not clear.

check.prompt: *Nos autem dicimus humanam uoluntatem sic diuinitus adiuuari ad faciendam iustitiam …* What follows *dicimus*?

quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A command addressed to the will.
An accusative and infinitive: *uoluntatem … adiuuari*, 'that the will is helped'.
A purpose clause with the gerundive *faciendam*.
check.explain: *dicimus* takes indirect statement. *humanam uoluntatem* is the subject in the accusative and *adiuuari* the passive infinitive. *ad faciendam iustitiam* is a gerundive phrase telling for what purpose the will is helped.

check.prompt: *ita uilia, ut nulla coloris uel habitus nouitate inter ceteros huius propositi uiros habeantur insignia.* What construction is this?

quoted.title: Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum)
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

options: A result clause: *ita … ut* with the subjunctive, 'so plain that they are not marked out by novelty of colour or style'.
check.explain: *ita* in the main part leads the reader to look for *ut*, and the subjunctive *habeantur* in the *ut* clause is a result: the clothing is so plain that nothing marks the monks out. Cassian repeats the pattern in the next clause (*ita … ut … sint …*).

reading.reference: John Cassian, Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum) 1.2.1 – John Cassian, Institutes (De institutis coenobiorum) 1.2.4
reading.why: Four short sections on the monk's clothing. They hold subjunctive relatives, *ita … ut* result clauses, passive verbs in a clause of 'whatever', and a word that the author explains himself. They are a good place to practise the routine: read, mark, ask for help in order, list.
